newsitem.title: FRANCE: French pension at 55 ups cost 117 bln Ffr - report.
newsitem.headline: French pension at 55 ups cost 117 bln Ffr - report.

text.p: Reducing the French retirement age to 55 from 60 could cost as much as 117 billion francs over 15 to 20 years, an unpublished study by the pensions branch of the social security system says, according to daily Les Echos.

The newspaper said a preliminary study by the CNAV branch of the social security system believed retirement across the board at 55 would add 2.8 million people to the pensioner population, raising existing claimers 31 percent from 9.1 million.

The CNAV estimated that the extra burden on the basic social security retirement benefit system in extra payouts would be in the region of 100 billion francs, plus 17 billion in foregone contributions from those retiring earlier.

The newspaper said "certain government experts" estimated that if a young person was recruited for each person departing at 55, the additional burden could be redcued to between 50 and 85 billion francs.
A recent poll by the BVA institute for BFM radio said 61 percent of French people favoured retirement at 55 but the idea has been rejected as totally unrealistic by the government.
It has been rejected by the opposition Socialists too and the idea of generalised earlier retirement has not got the support of the main trade unions either.

The newspaper noted that statistics from the INSEE national statistics institute forecasts that the proportion of people aged 55 or more in France will rise to 39.56 percent in the year 2050 from a little over 24 percent in 1995.

The recent controversy over earlier retirement follows a government agreement in December to allowing striking truck drivers quit at 55 as long as they have put in a minimum number of years of service and that those retiring are replaced by young staff.
The deal has been followed by sporadic claims for similar treatment in other sectors, mostly at local level.

The polemic also coincides with controversy over a bill, adopted after a second reading in the National Assembly on Wednesday, which would allow the creation of private pension funds in France alongside the traditional retirement benefit system funded by social security contributions and obligatory top-up schemes, ARRCO and AGIRC.

That bill, which would exempt employer payments into private pension funds from social security contributions and also offer tax relief to employers and employees, goes to the Senate on January 30 for a second reading.
